entries.title: What Should My Children Do? by Daniel Susskind review – the case for embracing tech in the classroom
entries.summary: A refreshingly optimistic book that asks us to grasp the educational opportunities of AI, rather than shrink from themIn 1979, the government asked Wilfred Cockcroft, a now largely forgotten maths lecturer from the University of Hull, to write a report about a crisis in the teaching of his subject to children. It was wide-ranging and meticulous, and included a chapter on a technological innovation
entries.content:
In 1979, the government asked Wilfred Cockcroft, a now largely forgotten maths lecturer from the University of Hull, to write a report about a crisis in the teaching of his subject to children. It was wide-ranging and meticulous, and included a chapter on a technological innovation that was suddenly becoming available to the average consumer: the calculator.

Many parents and teachers feared that the gadget would undermine a basic skill and a pillar of education – one of the sacred three Rs – producing generations of dumbed-down drones who could reach for a device in their pockets to avoid the hard graft of arithmetic.

But Cockcroft didn’t see it that way. Instead, he proposed embracing rather than fearing the calculator. Students should be taught with and without one – and tested accordingly.

“Cockcroft is unwilling to pretend that the oncoming wave of technological progress can be dodged,” economist Daniel Susskind writes in his urgent new book.

A former Downing Street policy wonk who is now also a researcher at the Institute for Ethics in AI at Oxford University, Susskind casts himself as the Cockroft of the 2020s. In an era of confusion and hand-wringing (if not outright panic) about the implications of AI, he makes the technologist’s case for breathing, learning and grasping the opportunities it presents.

The maths comparison only goes so far, of course; even accounting for the hubris of the AI industry, its achievements have already wrought changes that now make the calculator seem about as consequential as the corkscrew. But while the scale of the disruption is new, the historical context is, to some extent, reassuring.

The book’s title neatly taps into the techno-angst of the modern parent about a future of extreme uncertainty. If traditionally we passed down wisdom with an open-minded but fairly clear sense of how it might apply to a new generation, “today, it feels like that sense of continuity has broken. In truth, we cannot be sure the advice we gave our children last year still works for the next.”

Susskind, a father of young children himself, tries to anticipate a future of artificial general intelligence (AGI) – when AI will outperform us at every economically useful task. (We now have access, via ChatGPT, Claude and the like, to what’s known as artificial narrow intelligence: systems that are good at performing specific tasks.)

In an AGI world – one that it’s easy to imagine is round the corner after reading Susskind’s book –whole careers but also the very meaning of work will change. Susskind urges politicians, parents and teachers to start paddling into that wave now.

He warns against the folly of “future proofing” when the horizon is so foggy. He recalls the David Cameron government’s rush to teach kids how to code, just a few years before it emerged as one of the things that AI does best. Instead, schools should teach children to learn with and without AI, while also doubling down on the basic skills that we should never lose sight of.

He envisages a future of personalised learning, in which AI-trained teachers will deploy the technology as assistant tutors rather than attempting to cater to 30 children as a blob. Graduates entering white-collar industries that stand to be most disrupted should harness AI to free them from the drudgery of, say, reviewing legal documents in a basement and instead hone their craft earlier in AI-simulated trials. Middle-aged careerists should not “retreat to inherited practices” or kid themselves that they occupy “safe” professions; we must remember the underlying problem our professions seek to solve and reimagine how to do so in an AI-assisted age.

Susskind neatly weaves the conceptual and the practical. And while there was apparently no time in this slim work to consider the more immediate ethical implications of AI (its reliance on stolen creative work, its environmental toll) and the questionable personal qualities of so many AI bosses), as a call to action in the face of an unstoppable tide, his book is at once challenging, compelling and refreshingly optimistic.

entries.title: All About My Mother by Rachael Stirling review – a joyous love letter to Diana Rigg
entries.summary: Beautifully written by her daughter, this is a funny and intimate eulogy to the 60s star of The Avengers who went on to specialise in fierce, complicated womenThe late actor Diana Rigg declined to call herself a feminist, noting: “Why would I burn my bra? I need my bra.” Nonetheless, her ideas on womanhood were ahead of their time. In an interview with Michael Parkinson, she observed how marriage
entries.content:
The late actor Diana Rigg declined to call herself a feminist, noting: “Why would I burn my bra? I need my bra.” Nonetheless, her ideas on womanhood were ahead of their time. In an interview with Michael Parkinson, she observed how marriage was “all rather pagan, don’t you think? … A lot of women see it as security. Well, I’m not a woman who yearns for security.”

Taking over from Honor Blackman as the high-kicking Emma Peel in the 1960s spy series The Avengers, Rigg refused to play subordinate sidekick to Patrick Macnee’s Steed, turning her character into a beacon of female empowerment. When Rigg learned that not only was Macnee paid significantly more than she was, but the camera operator was too, she demanded a raise. She got it, but that didn’t stop the press from labelling her as a grasping diva. Fifty years later, she told Newsnight: “Equal pay. That’s what feminism means to me, only that.”

On the stage and screen, Rigg specialised in fierce, complicated women: Medea, Phèdre, Mother Courage, the wimple-clad Olenna Tyrell in Game of Thrones. Yet in life she refused to take herself or her job seriously. Her fear of appearing earnest led her to decline offers of a biography. Now, six years after her death from cancer, her daughter, the actor Rachael Stirling, has taken on the task of documenting Rigg’s life. All About My Mother is a funny, intimate, often joyous and beautifully written eulogy to a woman who didn’t suffer fools yet remained blithely self-mocking and down to earth. Asked what it meant to be made a dame, she replied: “I think it means I’m not supposed to say ‘fuck’ anymore.”

Blending memoir and biography, Stirling builds a portrait based on her own recollections, plus research into Rigg’s performances, writings, recorded interviews and press cuttings collected and stashed in a trunk by her late grandmother Beryl. The book, Stirling says, “is not a detached narrative … This is what I know, what she said, what I’ve learned, what I want to write, what she wrote and what I think she wouldn’t mind my telling you.”

Wild anecdotes of stars behaving badly include the time Rigg was lured to Benny Hill’s house with the promise of a party, only to find she was the sole guest. When he appeared in the garden proffering a drink and a semi-erect penis, Rigg turned away, shouted “LOOK! PARSLEY!” and scarpered. George Lazenby’s claim – false apparently – that Rigg deliberately ate garlic before their love scene in On Her Majesty’s Secret Service led to a scathing war of words between the two actors via a series of open letters.

As a youngster cutting her teeth on the stage, Rigg was a livewire: funny, rebellious, ambitious, given to corpsing from her own onstage pranks. Landing the role of Peel at 27, she found herself with a throng of male fans who wrote in their droves. Rigg put her mother in charge of letters, some of which took Beryl by surprise. She went to the police about a man who regularly sent clippings of his pubic hair in the post. “It turned out he had been bombarding loads of other women with the fruits of his bush,” notes Stirling. “How he managed to maintain his steady, seemingly luxuriant supply we will never know.”

As a mother, Rigg was doting and intense. She would weep dropping Stirling off at boarding school and in the holidays they were inseparable. “I suppose we became what you could call co-dependent, though I didn’t know the word for it then,” Stirling reflects. In a hilariously stomach-churning chapter called “Squeezums”, Stirling describes their ritual of zapping each other’s pimples using tweezers, a piece of loo paper and perfume as antiseptic.

Stirling followed her mother into acting, and Rigg could be fiercely critical of her daughter. On the rare occasions they performed together, Rigg would treat her less like a co-star than a personal assistant, though Stirling nearly always saw the funny side. Her book doesn’t shrink from her mother’s flaws and contradictions, but it remains, above all, a feel-good tale and a love letter. Now, before the first night of a new play, Stirling eats a grain of her mother’s ashes in order that “I am cloaked in her, shielded and shrouded by her. I am her. My mother is my superpower. She always was.”

All About My Mother by Rachael Stirling is published by John Murray (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: ‘She blazed in and opened my eyes to the real world’: Readers remember Gloria Steinem
entries.summary: To generations of women, the feminist campaigner was an inspiration, a fearless challenger of sexism and domestic violence. Guardian readers share memories of her courage, intelligence, and warmthWhat I appreciated most about Gloria was she let me feel normal. I graduated in engineering as one of three women in a class of over 150. In her world, a feminist was a woman that wanted to be judged for
entries.content:
‘She let me feel normal’

What I appreciated most about Gloria was she let me feel normal. I graduated in engineering as one of three women in a class of over 150. In her world, a feminist was a woman that wanted to be judged for her capabilities and not her gender. She was very inspirational and empowering when I first read her books as a young engineer. Teresa, Switzerland

‘A stalwart in my life’

She was a stalwart in my life and my evolution as a feminist and a supporter of the rights of women. I met Gloria Steinem once, at the very beginning of her career and of my own. Fresh out of Wellesley College, I travelled with a friend, another aspiring journalist, to cover the World Festival of Youth and Students, held in Vienna in the summer of 1959. The festival, it was widely acknowledged, was sponsored by the Soviet bloc; it came in the wake of the failed Hungarian revolt against communism and attracted young people from all over the world. From the US, there were two delegations, one called the New York group, the other the Cambridge crowd. Gloria Steinem was the super-glamorous, gorgeous, dynamic “secretary” of the Cambridge crowd. In her low-cut summer frock and what we called, even back then, “fuck-me sandals” she was a knockout, everywhere, directing operations, arranging for Ella Fitzgerald (no less) to give a free concert, feeding journalists stories, prompts, questions. I don’t think her official title was anything more than secretary, but clearly she was the person in charge. I was not surprised when she emerged several years later as a key figure in the burgeoning women’s movement. Her combination of brains and a well-nourished sense of humour brought strength, wit, and intelligence to the movement. And now, when we really need her like again, she is gone – but I pray her memory will continue to strengthen all of us who care about women’s lives and futures. Nancy Harmon Jenkins, 89, journalist, Camden, Maine

‘A lovely, gracious person’

In March of 2014, I was surprised to see Gloria Steinem got on my uptown 6 subway train here in NYC. It was fairly busy on the train but when someone offered her a seat she declined and said she was just going a couple of stops. She was very smiley and casual and even though it was likely most passengers in the car wouldn’t have known who she was, somehow it was clear everyone knew she was someone. This included a young woman who shyly approached her and they spoke for a few minutes and I should say Steinem looked thrilled to bits about this – just seemed like a lovely, gracious person and – like all true New Yorkers – happy to hop on the subway. Niko Wolf, New York City

‘I owe so much to her courage and strength’

Gloria blazed into my consciousness in high school, around 1975. She opened my eyes to the real world; I could define sexism and rail against it. In my 30s, my nickname, Little Miss Independent, surprised me. I was just living my life as I saw fit. She has given me a beautiful one, filled with love, joy, and travel. I owe so much to her courage and strength. I was blessed to come of age with her voice leading the way. I attended a talk held in a local school gym and travelled to the Woman’s March in DC in 2017. Her voice was manna from heaven. Jean, retired educator, New Jersey

‘The catalyst for my lifelong interest in gender studies’

I was attending Wichita State University in 1972 when Gloria Steinem spoke at a forum there. After she spoke she talked with some of us who attended. She was so warm and friendly. She inspired many of us to work to pass the ERA (equal rights amendment) even though it later failed. A year or two after meeting her I moved to Tehran, Iran. She certainly helped me have a different perspective on the living situations of women in Iran as well as the United States. She was very influential in my decision to study what was known then as women’s studies. She was the catalyst for my lifelong interest in gender studies and in particular issues and problems of middle-aged women around the world. Marlene Ammar, 81, Vancouver, Washington

‘My daughter was in awe’

Growing up in regional Queensland, reading Gloria Steinem’s books, it was like opening a portal to a new world that I wanted to be part of. I never met her but had the honour of hearing her speak on her final trip to Australia in May 2016 at Sydney town hall. I took my then 12-year-old daughter. She was in awe of Gloria, seeing all her books and hearing the excitement of the crowd while we waited for the hall to open. We became involved in some incredible conversations with women there – my daughter was incredulous to hear some of the stories such as [women] having to leave their jobs when they got married in the 1960s. We bought some of Gloria’s books and my daughter started to read them on the train home. It was a truly memorable evening. Toni Wren, 63, Sydney, Australia

‘Because of Steinem I became a domestic violence rescuer’

Because of Steinem I became a domestic violence rescuer after I saw how my mom was ignored by the system in the 1960s. I later helped pass the Violence Against Women Act in 1994. Gloria Steinem was a groundbreaking giant. She was smart and articulate like nobody before her, except Betty Friedan – we were so lucky to have these brave women. They woke us up from a long domestic violence nightmare. They did other things for women’s rights, but I appreciate her singular commitment in the DV space. Nobody was talking about it before. Rest in power Gloria, and thank you. Catherine, retired domestic violence worker, Seattle

‘That quick chat was the best’

When I graduated from high school in 1966, women were simply expected to get married, have babies, and work inside the home. I graduated from high school with honours; graduated from the University of Michigan with distinction; graduated from law school with honours; and passed the Michigan Bar Exam the first time I took it. After law school, I worked as a research attorney for two Michigan Circuit Court Judges and then practised with a highly respected, mid-sized law firm until my retirement. I was an early subscriber to Ms Magazine. I never knew Gloria Steinem and I only had the privilege to meet her once. Sometime during the 1990s, she was invited by the Michigan Bar Association to be a keynote speaker. I took a day off from work and drove myself across the state to attend the meeting. At the reception for Ms Steinem, I thanked her “for making my life so difficult”. She smiled and laughed and gave me a quick hug. And that was it. And even though I’ve met many important people, diplomats, and supreme court justices, that quick chat with her to thank her for helping me to fully become myself was the best. Lanie Anderson, 77, retired attorney, Bloomfield Hills, Michigan

‘Gloria was serious about representation’

My mother, Maya Miller, worked with Gloria on poverty and women’s issues. They were on the Ms Foundation board together, which was made up of a dozen or so women from across the country, across races and cultures – Gloria was serious about representation and knew a lot of very smart women. Most meetings happened back east in New York or DC, but in 1972 Nevada cut welfare payments in half. Knowing this affected mainly women and children, Gloria was one of several celebrities to come to Nevada to protest. There was a big march that shut down the Las Vegas strip. Gloria also came to northern Nevada to picket the legal brothels owned and run by men. Gloria supported my mother when Maya ran for US Senate from Nevada at a time when there were no women in the senate. I did meet her a few times, and remember her as kind. Kind eyes, soft spoken, and usually taking a back seat to listen to the other women in the room. And extremely smart with strategy, and witty at confronting chauvinism and stupid men. Kit Miller, 71, Washoe Valley, Nevada

entries.title: The Newer World by Sebastian Barry review – a near-miracle of storytelling
entries.summary: The third in a loose American trilogy follows the epic journey of a formerly enslaved man in the aftermath of the civil warBut is not the story as good as the truth?” asks Tennyson Bouguereau, the narrator of Sebastian Barry’s The Newer World. Tennyson, a formerly enslaved man in post-civil war America, recounts his life story in ways that call to mind the age-old debate about whether it’s better
entries.content:
But is not the story as good as the truth?” asks Tennyson Bouguereau, the narrator of Sebastian Barry’s The Newer World. Tennyson, a formerly enslaved man in post-civil war America, recounts his life story in ways that call to mind the age-old debate about whether it’s better to get our history from novelists or historians. While historians might argue that there is no contest, the question hints knowingly at the novelist’s counter-argument. It sent me searching for a line from Barry’s 2008 Costa-award winning novel, The Secret Scripture, in which the narrator describes history as “a fabulous arrangement of surmises and guesses held up as a banner against the assault of withering truth”.

In her Reith Lectures, Hilary Mantel suggested that history is “what’s left in the sieve when the centuries have run through it”, but I tend to think of it as more of a butterfly net. Historians chase after and capture the things they deem significant. They leave things out, often deliberately. Barry’s entire body of work is a prime example of fiction’s ability to fill history’s gaps, merging personal tragedies with national ones in ways that (dare I say) demonstrate the supremacy of the form – especially for those of us descended from people for whom history never cared one whit. I was therefore intrigued to learn that he had set out to write the story of a man like Tennyson. Barry’s earlier novels refracted Irish history through the lens of two fictional Irish families, the Dunnes and the McNultys. His first foray into this period of American history in Days Without End, for which he won his second Costa award, also followed one of the McNultys – Thomas McNulty flees the Irish famine for America, where he finds himself drawn into the genocidal work of clearing Native Americans off their land, and then, together with his lover and fellow soldier, John Cole, adopts a Lakota girl, Winona, whose family they have helped slaughter. Barry picked up Winona’s story in A Thousand Moons, published in 2020, which follows her fortunes as she, Thomas and John settle on the same farm outside Paris, Tennessee that is occupied by Tennyson and his twin sister Rosalee among others.

With the publication of The Newer World, it seems a loose trilogy has taken shape, hinting at possibilities for future expansion: the authorial hand nudging Tennyson from the background into centre stage and for the time being leaving the McNultys behind. This passing of the storytelling baton – an Irish refugee ceding the floor to a Native American woman, who then does the same in favour of a formerly enslaved man – feels as urgently contemporary as the best historical fiction always does, relevant to “the writer’s now”, to borrow John Fowles’s phrase. So too does the description of a postbellum Tennessee landscape in which the Confederates may have been defeated but their ideologies are still virulently alive: “All their intent was to shove us back into the hog pen and put the hasp on tight as they could, against any further straying”.

Part Bildungsroman, part picaresque, Tennyson’s account of himself moves from the American civil war, when “the end of the world had come”, to its immediate aftermath, “a time of guns and watchfulness”. He describes himself and Rosalee, enslaved orphans in childhood, “freed but not free” in adulthood, as “nothing people”. It’s reminiscent of Winona’s description of herself as “just the cinders of an Indian fire”, and Thomas’s of the ships bringing “ruined people” from Ireland to Canada: “The point is, we were nothing. No one wanted us.” The thing I like best about a Barry novel is how he gives a voice to the “nothing people” of history. It’s like pulling up a rocking chair on a shaded porch and listening as the narrator, usually in retrospective mode, attempts to reckon with what they did and what was done to them. It’s an astonishing effect, especially when you consider the near-miracles Barry performs with language. In his hands it attains registers that can only be described as soaring; a vertiginous high wire of prose. Here, for example, is Tennyson describing a reunion with his sister at sunset, after many years: “The harbour of my brave sister. The darkness growing in courage and, since it met no enemy, having its little victory everywhere. Pleasing darkness, in its way. There was bliss in those long moments”.

Putting this kind of arresting language into the mouths of “nothing people” makes it impossible to overlook them, as if only in fiction can they be given their due. And there is also a compelling point in using language from the poetic realm to reveal rather than cloak atrocities, its rhythms building to an unrelenting lyricism, a juggernaut that gains power precisely because it is not just set alongside brutality but entwined with it. Here is a siege, after Tennyson has enlisted in the army: “Men cried out as the life was lifted from them. All in the cruel dark.” Cruelty is endured and inflicted by the same people. In Days Without End, Thomas McNulty, an Irish famine victim, takes part in slaughtering Indigenous Americans; in The Newer World, Tennyson, an African American victim of enslavement, does the same. It is “never enough for Americans to live in their American paradise. There had to be blood and chaos all the while too.” What does it mean to be part of a “killing machine” where “[e]ven one death was a personal matter”?

I can think of no other writer who could, as Barry does, describe blood and chaos in language that reaches for such a high register, as if at the same time invoking paradise, in an attempt to answer that question. I can also think of few whose natural writerly empathy, evidenced by such an impressive body of work, pre-empts the otherwise inevitable discussion about cultural appropriation. Any writer has the right to imagine any point of view, but few truly earn it.

entries.title: The Castle by Jon Ronson review – bizarre tales of modern masculinity
entries.summary: A journalist embarks on a wild goose chase that might – or might not – be informative about the male conditionRecovering from surgery at home in upstate New York in 2023, Jon Ronson awoke to a string of texts from his adult son about a weird evening he just had at a stranger’s castle in Connecticut. Having gone along with a friend who’d been invited to a party there, he arrived to find a few lost-
entries.content:
Recovering from surgery at home in upstate New York in 2023, Jon Ronson awoke to a string of texts from his adult son about a weird evening he just had at a stranger’s castle in Connecticut. Having gone along with a friend who’d been invited to a party there, he arrived to find a few lost-looking young women with the sixtysomething host, Chris Mark, a steel heir filming a reality show about “101 princesses” whose first rule was “Never say no to King Chris”.

As a parent, Ronson is worried; as a reporter of more than 30 years on the cranks-and-crooks beat, he’s already on the clock. After trawling online whispers of sinister goings-on at the castle, he decides to pay a visit to Mark, who proudly shows off the stalactites and waterfall in his “cave-themed” bedroom before explaining how he picks up women on dating apps to “adapt” them to life as “princesses”. “The only girls that really work are drug addicts ... they don’t know what’s going on,” he says. Almost touchingly, Mark asks Ronson to sign an NDA, and the book describes Mark flooding his phone with threats when he declines.

Ronson knows he has a story on his hands; but what is it? A disenchanted associate leaks Mark’s private messages, revealing plans for a $2,500-an-hour floating brothel lit up in purple LEDs, and suggesting that Mark once paid for a woman to fly into the US from Poland, only for authorities to send her home in fear for her safety. Further dirt is dished by an ex-fiancee after Ronson two-facedly tells her he’s “really, really sorry” their relationship collapsed (he already told us “a break-up can be good news for a journalist”). As allegations mount, he imagines – perhaps even hopes – that Mark murdered his own father, who drowned in a boating accident in 2009.

While Ronson ends up satisfied Mark didn’t do that, the author’s willingness to guy his own ego – he wants “to be better than every other nonfiction writer” – adds a vital measure of comic charm to this creepy wild-goose chase. But gonzo sleuthing is only one ingredient of The Castle: the subtitle, Adventures in a World of Unravelling Men, hints at its ultimately piecemeal nature, as Ronson zigzags around case studies designed to illustrate the plight of the post-industrial male, simultaneously exhorted to open up and be vulnerable while pressured to avoid giving women “the ick” by snoring or failing to spot a beard crumb.

Boo hoo, one might counter, yet Ronson is persuasive on the problems of casting masculinity as original sin. He talks to an Australian man whose teacher rounded up every boy in his school to make them “apologise for rape”, and meets a lone father courted by YouTube for the lucrative videos he posted of his daughters’ food fights, then dropped when online Sherlocks wrongly accused him of kidnap.

Ronson makes these and other bizarre tales feel emblematic of topsy-turvy times, but when he says Chris Mark is just one of many men “discovering there were things they’d once done that they couldn’t do anymore”, you sense an over-caffeinated logic at work. “I was reminded a little of America in Iraq,” he tells us, when Mark can’t decide what to do with his castle, torn between housing OnlyFans models or setting up an orphanage. Mark’s “insatiable ... self-gratification” prompts a segment on the controversial actor Armie Hammer, seemingly mentioned only so Ronson can let us know Hammer gave him a tell-all scoop interview he didn’t publish.

Ronson’s reflexive parallels don’t always help us understand his slippery subjects. Mark also puts him in mind of the Father Ted co-creator Graham Linehan, an ex-friend whose online posts about transgender people Ronson compared to bullying, whereupon, he tells us, Linehan began subjecting him to multiple abusive messages. Ronson interviews him to try to fathom what fed his obsession, but it’s typical of The Castle’s jittery analytical style that Ronson’s eventual summing-up rests less on their six hours of video calls than on a tenuous analogy he detects in the tragic case of Brandi Bragg, a West Virginian teenager who fatally overdosed in 2004 after a lottery win plunged her into paranoia.

Near the end, he recounts the fatal shooting of Renée Good by an ICE agent who muttered “fucking bitch”. It isn’t clear why he brings this up, until he notes that Linehan – the only man in the book described as “unravelling” – apparently took to X to repost a tweet that called her “the face of chaos” and “the epitome of the modern-day liberal white woman”. “Graham’s plummet into disinhibition, his obsessive anti-wokeness, had evidently become so overwhelming it eclipsed his role as a self-appointed defender of women.” The gotcha, slipped into a footnote seven pages from the end, leaves you wondering if The Castle has been constructed not simply as an exploration of 21st-century maleness but as an act of slow-brew payback – though maybe it tells us something about men either way.

entries.title: Hawking by Graham Farmelo review – the dark side of genius
entries.summary: A biography of the physicist recognises his achievements, but also reveals the selfish narcissist underneathWhen I wrote an unadoring review of Stephen Hawking’s final book, a collection of essays published posthumously in 2018, New Scientist suppressed some of my criticisms on the grounds that it was “too early” to voice anything other than praise for the physicist who died, aged 76, that March.
entries.content:
When I wrote an unadoring review of Stephen Hawking’s final book, a collection of essays published posthumously in 2018, New Scientist suppressed some of my criticisms on the grounds that it was “too early” to voice anything other than praise for the physicist who died, aged 76, that March. It was apparently still too early in 2021, when no British publisher would touch Charles Seife’s exposé of Hawking’s bullying and self-aggrandising behaviour, Hawking Hawking.

In this new biography, veteran science writer Graham Farmelo takes a different approach. It is a comprehensive and accessible portrait of a brilliant scientist and an extraordinarily determined man who also possessed deep personal flaws to which the scientific community and the public mostly turned a blind eye. The uncomfortable but unavoidable truth is that Hawking’s overweening ambition and self-promotion, his repeated failure to acknowledge the work of others, his sexism and controlling behaviour were largely ignored because of his disability. I think it is indeed going to take us years to process that.

As this book was authorised by the Hawking family, and as Farmelo (whose superb biography of Paul Dirac, The Strangest Man, won a Costa award in 2009) is a generous and kind writer, I had feared the warts would be omitted. But instead Farmelo handles them mostly by letting others’ words speak for themselves.

But let’s start with the science, which offers a genuinely inspirational tale. As Farmelo says, while Hawking’s longevity against all odds was surely due in part to the exceptional care and treatment he received, “it was his unconquerable will, resilience and fortitude that did most to make his remarkable career possible”. His scientific achievements would be impressive by any measure; when accomplished in the face of debilitating and ultimately paralysing motor neurone disease, they are extraordinary.

Like many scientists of his calibre, Hawking was a slow and rather lackadaisical starter. But once installed at Cambridge for a PhD under the supervision of astrophysicist Dennis Sciama, his sharp intelligence emerged. It was there in early 1963 that, after a series of falls, he was diagnosed and given less than 10 years to live. Undeterred, and despite steadily declining mobility and speech, he was electrified by the work of physicist Roger Penrose, 10 years his senior, on the gravitational collapse of dead stars into what had become known as black holes.

That process was predicted by Einstein’s 1915 theory of general relativity, but Penrose was the first to show convincingly that it should lead to a “singularity” where all the star’s matter condenses to zero volume: an object with mass but no matter. Hawking had the brilliant insight that this same process, happening in reverse, could explain the big bang, in which the entire universe came into being from “nothing” 13.8bn years (as we now know) ago.

That was his first triumph, described in a 1970 paper with Penrose. The best came four years later, when Hawking proposed that, thanks to the peculiar quantum-mechanical nature of spacetime, black holes are not really black because they should constantly radiate a dim glow of particles – now called Hawking radiation – that will eventually lead to their evaporation. That work was a virtuosic blend of four fundamental ideas in physics: general-relativistic gravity, quantum mechanics, thermodynamics and information theory.

It was the high point of his research career: Hawking’s scientific achievements were largely done by the time he became a global celebrity, appearing on Star Trek and The Simpsons and becoming the subject of the 2014 Oscar-winning biopic The Theory of Everything. It is “as a truly great elucidator of black holes” that he will be remembered, Farmelo rightly judges.

I’m not alone in thinking Hawking’s work on black-hole thermodynamics and the discovery of Hawking radiation were worthy of a Nobel prize. (Hawking became obsessed to an unseemly degree with getting one.) But let’s keep it in proportion. Anyone who compares Hawking to Einstein knows nothing about Einstein or physics. Einstein made wide-ranging contributions to the discipline, but Hawking’s expertise was narrow and his forays outside it were sometimes embarrassing. Even in the closely related field of particle physics he said things that were, as Peter Higgs (of Higgs boson fame) said, “total crap”. “He made pronouncements about things he had no understanding of,” Higgs said – in the confident knowledge that it would make newspaper headlines the next day, uncritically lapped up by reporters.

Which brings us to the problematic stuff. While professional colleagues mostly spoke about Hawking with reverence and affection, it is often those closest to him who speak of another side. His father, Frank, worried that the teenaged Stephen “was developing into a selfish character … like a small boy who took everything but gave little in return”. There was evidently no love lost with his sister Mary, who called him “one of the most self-centred people I’ve ever met”. At Oxford, some friends found him rather lazy and entitled, and at Cambridge “annoyingly haughty”. His youngest son recounted how his father was “hugely competitive” and never let him or his siblings win at board games.

His unsparing ridicule of his first wife Jane’s religious beliefs contributed to their marital tensions, and the sacrifices she made often went unremarked by him. The pressure of going from lover to carer would never have been easy, but Hawking’s “authoritarian” demands and indifference to Jane’s interests added to her isolation. His adoptive brother, Edward, admitted “I’ve never really felt close to Stephen … he seems very cold.” And his mother, Isobel, complained how he would ignore people when it suited him. “I suppose what in other people would just be bad manners is excusable great-mannishness in him,” she wrote bitterly in her diary.

Sometimes the indulgence gets creepy. Who else’s Marilyn Monroe obsession would be pampered by hiring a lookalike to croon “I want to be loved by you” to him in a “whispery voice” on his birthday? What Farmelo calls “flirting” might have been seen as something else if Hawking had not been using a wheelchair. He does not mention the nights at Stringfellows strip club and makes light of the trip to (pre-conviction) Jeffrey Epstein’s island. But we do hear how Hawking’s victory in a scientific bet was celebrated by making his opponents deliver lectures in T-shirts showing scantily clad women. Hilarious.

Hawking was scandalously bad at giving due scientific credit to others, a trait evident from the outset when he failed to indicate his debt to Penrose. Worse was his treatment of physicist Jacob Bekenstein, whose idea about the connection between the area and the entropy of a black hole he mercilessly derided before discovering for himself that Bekenstein was right – and then essentially claiming the idea as his own, which Farmelo says “disappointed some of Stephen’s friends”. Hawking could clearly be a supportive and kind adviser to his own students, but when one discovered an argument for why Hawking was wrong about a conjecture concerning black holes, he tried to get him dismissed from the Cambridge PhD programme.

Some of his colleagues, Farmelo says, “believed that Stephen’s talks were ‘all about him’ and that he rarely gave much public credit to his peers”. Farmelo suspects they rarely grumbled because “such comments would have been interpreted as mean-spirited”. But mean-spiritedness rarely deters academics; what he surely means is mean-spirited about a scientist with a disability. And there’s the problem. If we were to start finally treating Hawking as we do any other scientist, it would be a positive step for disability in science (which is still poorly accommodated). The effect on Hawking’s legacy is another matter.

entries.title: Our Noble Selves by Kate Atkinson review – quirky postwar nostalgia from the Life After Life author
entries.summary: There are glimpses of Atkinson’s subtle brilliance in this gentle noirish mystery set around the Festival of BritainIn 1951, in a desperate attempt to raise the spirits of a shattered nation, the government came up with the Festival of Britain, a celebration of national creativity, grit and ingenuity. It is a moment in history that could have been designed for Kate Atkinson, who loves nothing more
entries.content:
In 1951, in a desperate attempt to raise the spirits of a shattered nation, the government came up with the Festival of Britain, a celebration of national creativity, grit and ingenuity. It is a moment in history that could have been designed for Kate Atkinson, who loves nothing more than a quirky detail and a cast of British eccentrics.

Harry Flynn (definitely think Errol), the quietly magnetic hero of Our Noble Selves, has survived Burma as a foreign correspondent turned war reporter. After a doomed marriage to a war widow called Ivy, and a stint in a mock-Tudor semi in Wealdstone with her, her eight-year-old daughter Veronica and a terrier, Mrs Betty, he resumes his bachelor life in London. A chance encounter with his old newspaper boss, Gerald Barry, leads him to a job compiling the festival’s poetry anthology. Barry provides a handy introduction: “The country’s stuck in the doldrums; we need to see the future,” he explains. The festival will celebrate “the Land and the People … Our love of country, love of freedom, love of nature, pride in craftsmanship, our reputation for tolerance and fair play.”

Flynn’s colleagues are mostly a likable bunch: there is 14-year-old Terence, “the Boy”, who behaves like “a motherly Cockney in a hammy play on the wireless”. There is “Badger”, rotund, affable and posh, something secret in the war; and Evans, a decent, melancholy, battle-scarred Welshman. When the team fall woefully behind schedule, Maud Ogilvie, a Scotswoman “beyond retirement age”, appears “from Typography” to sort them out. Anyone remotely familiar with Atkinson’s novels will know there’s no way a post-menopausal Scotswoman from typography is going to be a minor player.

As in Atkinson’s 2018 spy-themed novel Transcription, we are in a murky, plucky, postwar Britain that’s riddled with secrets. Atkinson’s method for controlling an extensive cast is to give each new character quirky identifying details. Individuals appear in Technicolored garb, sporting excellent period names (Flynn’s downstairs neighbours are elderly “spinster sisters” Hilda and Gertie Murgatroyd, who knit for the Distressed Gentlewoman’s Society). The signposting is rarely subtle. When a Mr Dangerfield appears at Flynn’s tea trolley, all military neatness and sinister jade eyes, and we learn that he’s a failed Tory candidate whose wartime stint in Secret Services didn’t “stick”, there’s really no need to wonder if he’s a wrong ’un.

A gentle noirish plot unfolds after Flynn has a date with the Parisian Delphine. That night, Delphine disappears but Flynn, inconveniently, has no memory of how the evening ended. He does wake up the next day, however, covered in blood.

Meanwhile, a competition to make the festival cake is won, inexplicably, by Mitzi Blinkhorn, a cartoonish ghoul in costume jewellery whose cake is repugnant. When her husband, Archie, appears, a skinny-legged “bantam cock” in a camel coat that indicates “a sleaziness of character”, we know there’s shady business afoot. It becomes clear that this is connected to Flynn’s increasingly alarming position as suspect No 1. His attempts to clear his name lead him into bed with the porcelain-skinned Lydia “who knows both Milton and more than one sexual position” and is, of course, more than she seems.

Flynn’s ex-stepdaughter Veronica, now a fearless 13-year-old, arrives at his flat bringing Mrs Betty (who, sadly, adds little) and helps him negotiate good-natured plot twists featuring colourful thugs, fillies and floozies, fascists and spies and good eggs. Devotees of Atkinson’s Jackson Brodie novels and of the more recent Shrines of Gaiety, with its big cast of London baddies, will probably love all this.

The background research provides a plethora of detail – you can’t go far in this novel without encountering a festival cow, a consignment of 208 plaster doves, or a room full of hopeful Nell Gwyns. Flynn admits to finding the Stock List (cricket bats, different kinds of Pyrex …) “soporific” and it’s hard to disagree; this is not an intellectually demanding fictional world, and a surfeit of details can clog the narrative.

There are glimpses, though, of Atkinson’s more subtle brilliance. She handles Flynn’s war trauma with a particularly deft touch: a well-chosen hint or two conveys more about hell and inner fragility than any exposition could. This is the Atkinson of Life After Life and A God in Ruins, her most sophisticated and powerful novels. Our Noble Selves doesn’t touch these in scope, structure or depth, but perhaps that isn’t the point. There is a gentle plea, here, for resilience and decency, couched in a nostalgia for a plucky and decent Britain that – if it ever existed – is certainly disappearing fast. Our prime minister might want to take notes. Hope lies in the willingness to celebrate difference; it lies in everyday kindness, a basic sense of right and wrong and in the willingness to be brave. In novel form, this can feel a bit twee but, when you think about it, Atkinson has a point.

entries.title: What we’re reading: Irvine Welsh, Janice Hallett and Guardian readers on the books they enjoyed in August

The tragedy is they are not
entries.content:
Irvine Welsh, author

I’ve been enjoying Contrapposto by Dave Eggers. The premise that love and art are the only things that make life worthwhile pulses beautifully through this novel and its two protagonists, spanning decades of their obsession with both, and each other. The tragedy is they are not sufficient alone for a relationship to survive to the exclusion of everything else (namely capitalism, which always has a place at the table), but they remain essential and enduring. Nowhere is this better evoked than here. Think John Williams’s Stoner but with art instead of literature and stuffed with more memorable characters.

In Raveheart, Graeme Armstrong confronts the twin promises of utopia and madness in a time before the internet’s colonisation of the mind, when people still dared to dream and lived to party. This book made me want to call some heads, rent a farmhouse, get a sound system and neck several pills. In fact, I might just do that.

Finally, another one for creatures of the night in all their disparate glory. Overnight by Dan Richards is more than a tribute to the people (and other critters) who operate in the hours of darkness to ensure we have everything we need – it’s a discourse on the very nature of night-time itself, and its essential relationship to our humanity. This is a beautifully written work of startling brilliance, astonishing the reader page after page.

Can Nothing Save Us? by Irvine Welsh is published by Jonathan Cape (£20). To support the Guardian, buy a copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

Jean, Guardian reader

I am reading The Shampoo Effect by Jenny Jackson. My only regret is not saving this book until my late summer beach vacation, because this book is best read with sand betwixt your toes. The story follows a group of lifelong friends in their thirties in their Massachusetts home town as they navigate marriage, parenthood, and careers. A newcomer from New York City arrives to work on what she hopes will be her big break as a writer and becomes irrevocably interwoven in the group’s complicated dynamics. It’s funny, sharp, and has me wondering as a child-free woman if many parents are self-medicating with weed on a regular basis to get through the day.

Janice Hallett, author

I’ve been diving deep into true crime lately. London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe is a book that examines so much more than its central crime story: that of a young man whose big dreams and relentless drive took him in a deadly direction. Keefe elevates the tragedy by placing it in the context of our capital’s criminal history. I’ve also revisited Carol Ann Lee’s exceptionally researched and presented The Murders at White House Farm.

For someone fascinated by criminal psychology and the legal system, this book is without a doubt a core text on the Jeremy Bamber case. Meanwhile, I was hooked for a whole weekend on Dead Fashion Girl by Fred Vermorel. Described as “a situationist detective story” it starts with the 1954 murder of a young fashion designer in Ruislip, not far from where I live, and splays outwards and downwards into London’s postwar criminal underbelly.

The Silent Appeal by Janice Hallett is published by Profile (£20). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

Barbara, Guardian reader

You wouldn’t think that an account of a ten-month long legal process would be a page-turner, but that is exactly what Emmanuel Carrère has achieved in V13, the book based on his weekly magazine columns covering the trial of the surviving perpetrators of the terror attacks in Paris on Friday (ie Vendredi) 13, 2015. He delves into the lives of the victims, the perpetrators, the lawyers, and produces an all-round picture of the human beings involved in this horrific event. It is written with compassion, empathy, and a genuine curiosity about motivation.

Light-years away (or perhaps not) is the deceptively simple tale told by Iain Crichton Smith in Consider the Lilies, a short novel about an elderly woman’s treatment at the hands of the Duke of Sutherland as he evicted tenants during the Highland Clearances – one woman, representing the fates of 150,000. A note at the front of the book tells me that I bought it on North Uist more than half-a-century ago, and now that I’m older I find it possibly even more moving than it was then.
